unit_label: CB Module C unit 4: liquidity management in the system (courseware unit 10)

facts.statement: Liquidity framework: concept and measures (courseware): the objective of liquidity management, which is the operating procedure of monetary policy, is to ensure adequate liquidity so that sufficient credit is provided to all productive sectors in the economy; a change in policy rate triggers the transmission of monetary impulses initially to the inter-bank call money market rate and thereafter to the longer-term interest rates on financial instruments including loans and deposits. Liquidity, in the sense used in the unit, refers to central bank liquidity: the reserves provided by a central bank to the banking system. Banks in many countries are required to maintain a mandated level of balances in their accounts with the central bank; these balances are referred to as required reserves; if the banking system has less money than the required reserve (which it needs to borrow from the money market), it is said that the system liquidity is in deficit and vice versa. Effective management of central bank liquidity operations is necessary since the variations in liquidity assume paramount significance in terms of their impact on major economic variables and on monetary policy operations: a shortfall of liquidity in the system causes interest rates to rise and the situation will be the opposite if the system experiences excess liquidity. Banking System Liquidity (BSL) measures: 1. Total borrowings of banks under LAF (TBBLAF) = all borrowings under repo/MSF/SLFMF (Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds); 2. Total of all reverse repo deposits (RRD); 3. Net borrowings of banks under LAF (NBLAF) = TBBLAF minus RRD; 4. AR = actual reserves maintained by banks with the Reserve Bank of India; 5. RR = required reserves (the statutory reserves required to be maintained by banks with the Reserve Bank of India); 6. ER (excess reserves maintained by banks with the Reserve Bank of India) = AR - RR; 7. BSL = NBLAF - ER; a positive figure of BSL indicates that the system liquidity is in deficit and (b) a negative figure for BSL indicates that the system liquidity is in surplus. Evolution of the LAF: the liquidity management framework of the Reserve Bank has evolved through progressive refinements since 1999; in April 1999 an interim liquidity adjustment facility (ILAF) was introduced under which liquidity was injected against collateral of Government securities at various interest rates, but surplus liquidity was absorbed at a fixed rate; a collateralised lending facility (CLF) was established alongside an additional collateralised lending facility (ACLF), with export credit refinance and liquidity support to primary dealers linked to the Bank Rate; the transition from ILAF to a full-fledged LAF took place in June 2000. LAF is a tool used in monetary policy formulation that allows banks to borrow money through repurchase agreements; this arrangement allows banks to receive funds in times of liquidity pressures for the purpose of ensuring stability in the operations of the financial markets; banks use their eligible securities as collateral and obtain funds from the central bank through a repo agreement. LAF was introduced in India in two stages: the first stage was introduced effective June 5, 2000; under this scheme, a flexible repo rate was put in place, countering the earlier fixed rate repo; the reverse repo rate was placed a notch higher than the repo rate to push up short-term rates of interest with a view to maintaining orderly conditions in the foreign exchange market; the non-bank financial institutions who were participants in the inter-bank call money market were permitted to lend, on an average, up to 85 per cent of their average daily call money lending; the second stage of LAF was introduced effective May 8, 2001, with some refinements: under this scheme, banks were allowed to borrow normal liquidity at the Bank Rate and a backstop facility at variable daily rate at 1 percentage point above the reverse repo cut-off rate in LAF auctions or 200 to 300 basis points above the repo cut-off rate; the normal facility would be about two-thirds and the backstop facility about one-third of the total limits of standing liquidity support to banks and primary dealers in government securities; export credit refinance was allowed up to certain specified limits. Internal Group on Liquidity Adjustment Facility (Chairman D. Anjaneyulu, Principal Monetary Policy Adviser, 2003): the report was placed on the website on December 2, 2003; as a result the revised scheme was operationalised through (i) 7-day fixed rate repo conducted daily and (ii) overnight fixed rate reverse repo conducted daily on weekdays; the existing overnight variable rate repo auction facility would be available to eligible market participants up to April 2, 2004; subsequently the overnight repo auction would be discontinued and only the 7-day repo would be available; the 14-day repo, conducted on a fortnightly basis, will also be available; the entire amount under the Standing Liquidity Facilities (SLF) was to be made available at a single rate (the repo rate); a normal facility and back-stop facility were to be merged; the Reserve Bank decided to switch over to fixed rate repos on an overnight basis and introduce longer term repos up to 14-day period as and when required. With the introduction of LAF, steering overnight money market rates emerged as the key challenge; the LAF was operated through overnight fixed rate repo (rate at which liquidity is injected) and reverse-repo (rate at which liquidity is absorbed) from October 2004; the repo rate was the ceiling and the reverse-repo rate the floor of the corridor; the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) was introduced in April 2004 to offset the excess liquidity from large capital inflows. The Working Group on Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy (March 15, 2011) recommended that the repo rate should be the single policy rate and reverse repo rate and the Bank Rate follow; Box 10.1: the key recommendations: the liquidity adjustment facility with some modifications should be the key element in the operating framework; the modified LAF should operate in a deficit liquidity mode with the liquidity level contained around (+)/(-) 1 per cent of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL); the Bank Rate be reactivated as a discount rate at which the Reserve Bank will provide liquidity under a new collateralised Exceptional Standing Facility (ESF) up to 1 per cent of NDTL of banks to be carved out of the required SLR portfolio; the reverse repo rate will have a negative spread on the repo rate, and it will be the rate at which the Reserve Bank will absorb liquidity under the LAF; the reverse repo rate will constitute the lower bound of the corridor; the optimal width of the policy corridor should be fixed at 150 basis points; the weighted average overnight call money rate should be the operating target of monetary policy; the minimum level of reserves to be maintained on any day by banks during a fortnight should be raised from the present level of 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the required CRR; the Reserve Bank should conduct second LAF (SLAF) on a regular basis; a scheme for auctioning of surplus cash balance of the Government.

Revised LAF frameworks (courseware): the Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework (Chairman: Urjit R. Patel, 2014) recommended that excessive reliance of the Reserve Bank on the overnight segment of the money market should be avoided by de-emphasising overnight variable rate repos and instead liquidity management operations should be conducted through term repos of different tenors; the Committee recommended design changes and refinements in the operating framework of LAF; flexibility in the use of instruments; the key change in the framework was doing away with unlimited accommodation of liquidity needs at the fixed LAF repo rate; other important elements of the revised framework: (i) provision of the predominant portion of central bank liquidity through regular term repos; (ii) introduction of fine-tuning operations through repo/reverse repo auctions of maturities varying from overnight to 28 days with liquidity assessment undertaken on a continuous basis; and (iii) phasing out export credit refinance. The liquidity management framework adopted by the Reserve Bank in 2014 proved to be robust and resilient during the demonetisation period; the Internal Working Group (IWG) on liquidity management framework was constituted on June 6, 2019 with a mandate to review the current liquidity management framework with a view to simplifying it and suggest measures to clearly communicate the objectives and the toolkit; the report was published on September 26, 2019. Recommendations of the IWG: corridor versus floor system (the corridor system affords the desired flexibility to manage situations of liquidity deficit as well as liquidity surplus and given that the repo rate is the policy rate set by the MPC, the Group recommends that the liquidity management framework should continue to be based on the corridor system); call money rate as the target rate (as the call money market is the only money market segment which trades exclusively in reserves, the Group recommends that the call money rate with weighted average call rate (WACR) as the measure should continue as the target rate of the liquidity management framework); the desired level of system liquidity: with the repo rate as the policy rate, the corridor system would generally require the system liquidity to be in a small deficit of about 0.25 per cent to 0.5 per cent of NDTL of the banking system; if financial conditions warrant a situation of liquidity surplus the framework could be used flexibly, with variable rate operations to ensure that the call money rate remains close to the policy repo rate; managing day-to-day liquidity (uncertainty, if any, about the Reserve Bank liquidity management should be minimised by conducting operations at a rate close to the policy repo rate; the daily primary liquidity management operation should be ideally one single overnight variable rate operation; the liquidity framework should entirely meet the liquidity needs of the system, so a separate provision of assured liquidity is no longer necessary); Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs) should be allowed to participate directly in all overnight liquidity operations; the Reserve Bank should stand ready to undertake intra-day fine-tuning operations, if necessary, but such operations should be the exception to address unforeseeable intra-day shocks rather than the rule; managing durable liquidity: under the corridor system, build-up of liquidity in a large deficit (greater than about 0.25 per cent to 0.5 per cent of NDTL) or surplus, if expected to persist, should be offset through appropriate durable liquidity operations (OMO purchases or sales, buy/sell forex swaps); the Group recommended longer-term variable rate repos of more than 14 days and up to one-year tenor and longer-term variable rate reverse repos as new tools; the boundaries of the corridor system: the Group recommends that the current difference of 25 basis points between the repo rate and the reverse repo rate, as well as between the repo rate and the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate, be retained; margins: margin requirements under the LAF should be reviewed periodically and the margin requirement for reverse repo transactions should continue to be Nil; reserve averaging: the present minimum requirement of maintaining 90 per cent of the prescribed CRR on a daily basis has helped avoid bunching of reserve requirements of individual banks; the Group recommends that this minimum requirement be retained at the present level; the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), a tool to absorb liquidity, may be operationalised early; communication and disclosures: Money Market Operations press release modified to show both the daily flow impact as well as the stock impact of the Reserve Bank liquidity operations, and a quantitative assessment of durable liquidity conditions of the banking system published on a fortnightly basis with a lag of one fortnight. Revised framework based on IWG (10.5): the weighted average call rate will continue to be the operating target; with the WACR being the single operating target, the need for specifying a one-sided target for liquidity provision of one percent of NDTL was removed and the daily fixed rate repo and four 14-day term repos conducted every fortnight were withdrawn; a 14-day term repo/reverse repo operation at a variable rate conducted to coincide with the cash reserve ratio (CRR) maintenance cycle was made the main liquidity management tool for managing frictional liquidity requirements; the main liquidity operation would be supported by fine-tuning operations; overnight and/or longer, to tide over any unanticipated liquidity changes during the reserve maintenance period; Standalone Primary Dealers were allowed to participate directly in all overnight liquidity management operations. Structuring of OMOs: central banks appropriately evolve structured OMOs keeping in view the market requirements of liquidity in terms of duration as well as quantum; in India the OMO structures are evolved using Central and State Government Securities of different maturities; the relevant bonds could range from 1 year to 20/30 years; Treasury Bills of 7, 14, 28, 91, 182 and 365 days are ideally used; repo operations are part of OMO; when the central bank sells securities it withdraws liquidity from the market and when it repurchases it injects liquidity; reverse repos absorb. The IWG: the banking liquidity being kept in deficit or surplus mode is a design feature; whether the corridor system or the floor system; the choice between the two systems, therefore, depends on the prevailing liquidity climate; fixed and variable rate operations; for ensuring activity in the inter-bank money market, banks should have the incentive to trade among themselves rather than with the central bank: banks should be able to borrow in the inter-bank market at rates not higher than the rate at which they could borrow from a central bank and lend at rates not below the rate at which they could lend to a central bank.

Liquidity management during Covid-19 and recent measures (courseware): in response to Covid-19, the Reserve Bank deployed several conventional and unconventional tools; the policy repo rate has been lowered by 135 bps since March 2020, taking the size of cumulative rate cuts to 250 bps since February 2019; the system liquidity, which was in slight deficit at the start of 2019, turned into surplus by May 2019; the surplus increased to Rs 1 lakh crore on a net average daily basis, starting July 2019 and expanded manifold since then; starting February 2020, the Reserve Bank was absorbing around Rs 3 lakh crore from the banking system on a daily average basis; the monetary policy committee (MPC) met off-cycle on March 24 to 27 and May 20 to 22, 2020, and voted to reduce the policy rate by 115 bps, over and above the reduction of 135 bps during February 2019 to February 2020, bringing the cumulative reduction in the policy rate to 250 bps (as the courseware says); measures aimed at boosting (1) system level liquidity (2) sector specific funding (3) institution level liquidity; and (4) instrument level liquidity. Money markets: the money markets have remained flush with surplus liquidity due to the Reserve Bank support through LAF operations; the net LAF position was around Rs 3.0 lakh crore on an average, during Q4: 2019-20, increased to an average of Rs 4.7 lakh crore during Q1: 2020-21 (up to June 22, 2020); the Reserve Bank has had to engage in daily absorption operations with the average deposit of funds in the overnight reverse repo window increasing more than three times, from an average of Rs 2.4 lakh crore to Rs 7.0 lakh crore during the same period; due to abundant surplus liquidity the weighted average overnight money market rate (WAMM) has hugged the bottom of the policy corridor, reverse repo rate rather than the repo rate; the tri-party repo (TREPS) and market repo rate have consistently remained lower than the reverse repo rate since March 2020. The Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd (IL&FS), a non-banking finance company (NBFC), defaulted on its commercial paper (CPs) obligations in August 2018; this default brought the funding structure and asset liability mismatches of NBFCs under scrutiny, and these concerns got extended to housing finance companies (HFCs) after the collapse of a large housing finance company in 2019, namely DHFL (another NBFC) which defaulted towards funds it raised heavily from PSBs and also borrowed heavily by issuing bonds and other debt instruments to retail investors; the resultant default/contagion fears led to an equity market sell-off and brought the focus on NBFCs (including HFCs), especially their exposures, adverse selection of assets and funding of long-term assets with short-term liabilities. The Reserve Bank acted with a sense of urgency and provided support by permitting commercial banks to provide partial credit enhancement to bonds issued by select NBFCs and HFCs, permitting banks to reckon government securities held by them up to an amount equal to their incremental outstanding credit to NBFCs and HFCs as Level-1 high quality liquid assets (HQLA), and increasing the pace and quantum of liquidity infusion via open market operations (OMOs) and term repos; the list of eligible borrowers for external commercial borrowings (ECBs) was also expanded to include HFCs and the average maturity requirement for ECBs in the infrastructure segment was reduced from 5 years to 3 years. Corporate bond market liquidity: the Reserve Bank announced Targeted Long Term Repo Operations (TLTROs) on March 27, 2020 for Rs 1.0 lakh crore to address higher illiquidity premia in the corporate bond market; the 3-year funds availed by the banks under this facility had to be deployed in fresh acquisition of investment grade corporate bonds, CPs and Non-convertible Debentures (NCDs) in both primary and secondary segments of the markets; the Reserve Bank announced TLTRO 2.0 on April 17, 2020, to channelise liquidity to small and mid-sized corporates, including NBFCs and micro finance institutions (MFIs); funds availed under TLTRO 2.0 were deployed in investment grade bonds, CPs and NCDs of NBFCs; it was mandated that at least 50 per cent of the total funds availed under the facility would have to be invested in the securities of MFIs and smaller NBFCs; the Reserve Bank provided special refinance facilities for a total amount of Rs 65,000 crore to the AIFIs, viz., NABARD, SIDBI, NHB and EXIM Bank to enable them to meet the sectoral credit needs of the economy; Long Term Repo Operations (LTROs) in February 2020 (the Reserve Bank announced revised framework and additional liquidity infusion through Long Term Repo Operations (LTROs) of 1-year and 3-year tenor in the Statement on Regulatory and Developmental policies of February 06, 2020); Operation Twists (simultaneous purchase of longer-dated securities and sale of shorter-tenor securities) were announced; the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF-MF): in March-April 2020 mutual funds faced redemption pressure due to volatility in capital markets; the Reserve Bank announced a Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds with several regulatory benefits; the funds availed under SLF-MF were to be used by banks exclusively for meeting the liquidity requirements of MFs and preserving liquidity in the market; on April 30, 2020, the regulatory benefits announced under the SLF-MF scheme were extended to banks, which deployed their own resources. Government securities market and the risk-free curve: the first point of call in the transmission of changes in the policy rate is the inter-bank call money rate; subsequently this impulse gets transmitted to longer term risk-free interest rates and other traded financial instruments, and finally to loan and deposit rates; the Reserve Bank conducted special OMOs involving simultaneous purchase of longer-dated securities and sale of short-tenor securities (Operation Twist) on December 19, 2019. Equity markets: in March 2020, the Indian equity markets witnessed record net FPI outflow of Rs 62,000 crore (USD 8 billion approximately), followed by an outflow of Rs 6,340 crore in April 2020; the return of FPIs in May and June 2020. Recent measures announced by RBI on 08 April 2022: the introduction of a standing deposit facility (SDF) at 3.75 per cent which would serve as the floor for the policy corridor; with this, the width of the policy corridor was narrowed to 50 basis points (bps) from 65 bps; the SDF will allow the absorption of liquidity from the system without requiring banks to provide any collateral in exchange; unlike other liquidity instruments which are administered at the discretion of the RBI, the use of the SDF and the MSF will be left to the discretion of banks and will be available after market hours on all days of the week; the marginal standing facility (MSF) at the upper end of the policy corridor at 4.25 per cent; the Reserve Bank moved away from ultra-accommodation, i.e., withdrawal of support already provided during the pandemic; the Reserve Bank also raised the ceiling for government securities that can be held to maturity (HTM) to 23 per cent from 22 per cent up to March 31, 2023; the restoration of the 19.5 per cent cap on HTM securities will be made in a phased manner starting from Q1FY24 ending with Q4 FY24; when a larger share of securities is moved into the HTM basket, the supply of paper in the market is reduced to that extent, thus supporting bond prices.

payload.title: Liquidity, system liquidity measures and the evolution of the LAF
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why:** liquidity management is the **operating procedure of monetary policy**. A **policy rate** change first moves the **inter-bank call money rate**, then **longer-term rates**, **loan and deposit rates**.

**Meaning:** **central bank liquidity** = **reserves** the central bank provides to banks. Banks must hold **required reserves (RR)**; if the system has **less than required**, liquidity is in **deficit**; more means **surplus**. A **shortage raises rates**; **excess lowers** them.

**Banking System Liquidity (BSL):**

- **TBBLAF** = total borrowings under **repo, MSF and SLF-MF**;
- **RRD** = **reverse repo deposits**; **NBLAF = TBBLAF − RRD**;
- **AR** = actual reserves; **RR** = required reserves; **ER = AR − RR** (excess reserves);
- **BSL = NBLAF − ER**. **Positive BSL = deficit; negative BSL = surplus.**

**Evolution:** **April 1999 ILAF** (injection against government securities; surplus absorbed at a **fixed rate**; **CLF/ACLF**, export credit refinance and PD support linked to the **Bank Rate**) → **full LAF from June 2000**.

- **Stage 1 (5 June 2000):** **flexible repo rate**; reverse repo **above** the repo rate; non-bank lenders in call money allowed to lend up to **85 per cent** of average daily lending.
- **Stage 2 (8 May 2001):** a **normal facility** at the **Bank Rate** (about **two-thirds**) and a **backstop facility** (about **one-third**) at **200-300 bps above repo**.

**Internal Group on LAF (2003, chaired by D. Anjaneyulu):** daily **7-day repo** and **overnight reverse repo**, a **14-day repo** fortnightly, merging normal and backstop facilities into **one facility at the repo rate**; from **October 2004** **overnight fixed-rate repo (ceiling) and reverse repo (floor)**; the **MSS (April 2004)** absorbed capital inflow liquidity.

**Working Group on Operating Procedure (15 March 2011):** **repo rate as the single policy rate**; **WACR** as **operating target**; **corridor** of **150 bps** (repo + 50, reverse repo repo − 100); **Bank Rate reactivated** with an **Exceptional Standing Facility** up to **1 per cent of NDTL**; liquidity around **±1 per cent of NDTL**; minimum daily reserve **from 70 to 80 per cent of CRR**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The framework moved from an injection facility to a corridor around a single policy rate.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the formula for Banking System Liquidity (BSL)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: BSL = net borrowings under LAF minus excess reserves; a positive value means a deficit.

payload.title: Later revisions: Patel Committee (2014) and the Internal Working Group (2019)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Patel Committee (2014):** avoid **reliance on overnight variable rate repos**; **term repos of different tenors** provide the **bulk of liquidity**; **end unlimited accommodation at the fixed repo rate**; **fine-tuning repos/reverse repos** (**overnight to 28 days**); **phase out export credit refinance**.

**Internal Working Group (IWG, constituted 6 June 2019, report 26 September 2019):**

- **Corridor** (not floor) system continues.
- **WACR** remains the **operating target**.
- Desired system liquidity: a **small deficit of about 0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL**; use **variable rate operations** if surplus arises.
- **Day-to-day:** one **overnight variable rate operation** at a rate **close to the repo rate**; **no separate assured liquidity**; **standalone primary dealers** may take part directly; **intra-day fine-tuning** only for **unforeseen shocks**.
- **Durable liquidity:** build-ups beyond **0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL** should be offset by **OMOs, forex swaps** and **longer-term (above 14 days up to one year) variable rate repos and reverse repos**.
- **Corridor edges:** **25 bps** between **repo and reverse repo** and between **repo and MSF** retained; **margins** reviewed (reverse repo margin **nil**); **reserve averaging**: **90 per cent of CRR on a daily basis** retained; the **SDF** to be operationalised early; **communication**: **Money Market Operations** release to show **daily flow and stock impact**, and a **fortnightly durable liquidity assessment**.

**Revised framework in practice:** with **WACR** as the single target the **one-sided liquidity target was removed**; the **daily fixed rate repo and the 14-day term repos were withdrawn**; a **14-day term repo/reverse repo at a variable rate**, timed with the **CRR maintenance cycle**, became the **main liquidity tool** (with **fine-tuning operations**).

**Principles:** deficit or surplus is a **design choice**; **fixed rate operations** when **normal**, **variable rate** for **unanticipated** conditions; **banks should prefer trading among themselves** (borrow in the inter-bank market at no more than the **central bank lending rate** and lend at no less than the **central bank borrowing rate**).

**OMO structure:** **government securities of 1 to 20/30 years** and **Treasury Bills (7, 14, 28, 91, 182, 365 days)**; **repos** inject, **reverse repos** absorb.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The IWG kept the corridor and made a 14-day variable rate operation the main tool.

self_check.prompt_text: Which operation became the main liquidity management tool after the IWG recommendations?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A 14-day term repo/reverse repo at a variable rate, timed with the CRR maintenance cycle.

payload.title: Liquidity measures during Covid-19 and the April 2022 SDF
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Context:** from **February 2019** the **repo rate was cut by 250 bps cumulatively** (135 bps before and **115 bps off-cycle in March-May 2020** by the MPC); system liquidity turned to **surplus from May 2019** and the Reserve Bank **absorbed large amounts daily**. **Measures targeted four levels:** **system**, **sector**, **institution** and **instrument** liquidity.

**Money market:** **abundant surplus** kept the **overnight rate** near the **reverse repo rate (the bottom of the corridor)**; **TREPS and market repo** traded **below the reverse repo**.

**NBFC/HFC stress:** **IL&FS defaulted on its commercial paper in August 2018** and **DHFL** in **2019**; the Reserve Bank allowed **partial credit enhancement by banks**, counted **government securities as Level-1 HQLA** up to **incremental credit to NBFCs/HFCs**, added OMOs and term repos, widened **ECB eligibility to HFCs** and cut the **ECB infrastructure maturity from 5 to 3 years**.

**Tools:** **Long Term Repo Operations (LTROs)** of **1 and 3 years (February 2020)**; **Targeted LTROs** (**27 March 2020**) with funds used for **investment grade corporate bonds, CP and NCDs**; **TLTRO 2.0 (17 April 2020)** with **at least 50 per cent** in **MFIs and smaller NBFCs**; **special refinance of Rs 65,000 crore** to **NABARD, SIDBI, NHB and EXIM**; **Operation Twist** (buy long, sell short government securities, **December 2019**); **Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF-MF)** in **March-April 2020**.

**Risk-free curve and transmission:** the call money rate moves first, then **risk-free longer rates**, then **loan and deposit rates**.

**8 April 2022:** the **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** at **3.75 per cent** became the **floor** (corridor narrowed from **65 to 50 bps**); it **absorbs liquidity without collateral**, and **use is at banks' discretion**, **available after market hours on all days**; **MSF** at **4.25 per cent** is the **ceiling**. The Reserve Bank **moved away from ultra-accommodation** and raised the **held-to-maturity ceiling to 23 per cent** (from 22 per cent) until **31 March 2023**, with the **19.5 per cent cap restored in phases through FY24**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The pandemic response combined policy rate cuts with targeted liquidity to specific markets and sectors.
